old:
\begin{abstract}
This manuscript presents a candidate proof that the unit circle is a
natural boundary for the zero-field, isotropic, infinite square-lattice
Ising susceptibility continued from low temperature. The argument has
two separate analytic tasks. At a dense cyclotomic family of boundary
points, an actual average-angle residue produces a nonzero first
singular derivative. A weighted contour deformation and a partition of
the entire particle-number tail are then used to claim an absolute
smaller-order bound for every derivative needed in the bulk product
rule. The decisive estimates, support conditions, differentiation
recurrences, and order of choices are included in the paper.

This release candidate is reconstructed from an AI-generated research checkpoint.
Its propositions are the proof claims to be checked, not independently
certified results. Appendix~\ref{app:auditmap} identifies the load-bearing
checks and the coverage of all tail sectors. No exhaustive priority
clearance is claimed; the natural-boundary conclusion has no
independent human certification. This revision proves the required
lower-order radial bounds internally, strengthens the selected-contour
pair bound, evaluates the singular coefficient, and records a finite-order
obstruction to smooth extension on every boundary arc. It also identifies
the complete selected-point amplitude relative to the literature
formula, including its four-chart degeneracy and physical branch. The corresponding
Lean candidate is version 0.3.0-rc2; the frozen 0.1-rc4 manuscript and
0.2.1 Lean release retain their separate identities.
\end{abstract}
new:
\begin{abstract}
The unit circle is a natural boundary for the normalized zero-field
susceptibility of the isotropic infinite square lattice, continued from
the low-temperature ordered pure phase. The proof isolates a nonzero
singular derivative at a dense cyclotomic family of boundary points and
shows that the complete higher-particle tail is smaller in every
derivative required by the product rule. The first term is evaluated by
an average-angle residue followed by a convergent shape integral. The
tail is controlled by an exact weighted contour deformation, protected
parameter disks, and a partition covering every particle number and
angular region. The paper includes the support conditions, high-order
differentiation recurrence, and order of parameter choices on which
these estimates depend.

The physical interpretation retains the onsite contribution, the
magnetization-square subtraction, and the full positive even-particle
sum. It uses the published low-temperature correlation representation
and spontaneous magnetization as explicit physical inputs. The analytic
construction itself, including the lower-order radial bounds, is
internal. We also give a selected-point amplitude evaluation, its
four-chart literature comparison, and a finite-order obstruction on
every boundary arc. These last scalar and covering calculations have
the manuscript-only scope recorded in Appendix~\ref{app:auditmap}.
That appendix also records the precise Lean endpoint and the source
and AI-assistance provenance of this reader edition.
\end{abstract}

\subsection{Construction details retained in this edition}
The present proof uses the first nonzero-angle prime family and all
thirteen tail sectors. Its real-cutoff recurrence, hybrid measures,
constant choices, and separate radial-center and protected-disk
arguments are given in full. In exterior convergence, the inverse
products cost an exponential factor in \(N\); the
Pfaffian--factorial bound absorbs that factor, and compact-set Cauchy
estimates give differentiated normal convergence. In the original disk,
the real branch-center displacement includes the complex parameter
perturbation \(|s-\se|\). The two-region estimate retains it and yields the
occupancy-independent integrable majorant.

The first-term calculation uses a partition depending only on the
\(y\) angles, followed by \(x\) residues, separated mean-edge replacements,
and a finite-cover complement estimate. The support construction retains
compact upper supports and branch plateaus, and its periodic seam lies
where all relevant weighted jets vanish. Cauchy's inequality is applied
to the complete holomorphic selected integral \(F_N\). The exponential support
inclusions hold at every finite tail order, including the negative
anchor scale. The microcore logarithm retains its negative
\(N^2\log N/2\) term. Near-equality coarea retains the
unwrapped phase lengths and their period counts. The ordered \(+\) pure-phase
convention and the full-site/offsite normalization are explicit.

The complete-pair estimates assert strictness within groups and allow
cross-group equality. Their continuation uses the actual supports,
reserved disk slack, restrictions depending on the deformation strength,
and the coupled-occupancy product-rule count. The original-disk pair
estimate applies to the \(K\) and named-current supports. The current
partition, deformed branch geometry, remaining-pair count, near-collision
slope cost, and ordered constants are included, with \(N\) restricted to its stated
window. The proof does not use
a jointly absolute mean/shape limit, division by the original
Vandermonde, a central connector contour, or a degenerate four-particle
endpoint amplitude. Inverse temperature and the inner branch cutoff
remain distinct from the geometric angle \(\beta\).

\subsection{Formal scope and physical identification}
The original Lean source proves the natural-boundary theorem for the
constructed normalized exterior series without an external physics
premise. Its canonical first-term and final dependency chain includes
the internal lower-order radial bound; the former external regularity
input E3 is absent from that chain. The stronger selected-contour pair
bound is also represented in the source. The physical interpretation
uses the explicit E1 correlation representation in the \(+\) state and
the E2 magnetization identity.

and the explicit premises \texttt{PhysicalSusceptibilityE1} and

 double-contour, full offsite, and full-site coefficients are retained
